text: A comet is a lump of ice, dust and rock, often called a dirty snowball. Most spend their lives far from the Sun, in the cold outer solar system. When one swings close to the Sun, its ice turns to gas and blows off, forming a glowing head and long tails that can stretch for millions of kilometres.

A few comets have become famous. Halley's Comet is the best known, because it returns roughly every 76 years. Others became famous for one dazzling visit, like Hale-Bopp in 1997, or for something dramatic, like Shoemaker-Levy 9, which smashed into Jupiter.

st.prompt: Which way does a comet's tail point?

options.t: Away from the Sun
Behind the comet, opposite to the way it is moving
Towards Earth

st.reveal: Sunlight and the solar wind push the comet's gas and dust outward. So the tail always points away from the Sun, even when the comet is heading back out into space tail first.

myth: Comets are fireballs burning as they fly through space.
Comets are cold lumps of ice, dust and rock, a few kilometres across. Their glowing heads and tails form when sunlight warms the ice and turns it to gas, which then reflects sunlight and glows.

sec.t:
People had seen this comet for thousands of years without knowing it was the same one coming back. In 1705, the English astronomer Edmond Halley worked out that comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 followed the same path. He predicted a return in 1758. He died before it arrived, but it came, and it was named after him.

Halley's has been spotted in records going back over 2,000 years. In 1066 it appeared before the Battle of Hastings in England. It is stitched into a famous embroidered cloth, about 70 metres long, made in the 1070s to tell the story of that war. Medieval people in [[@knights-castles|castles]] and villages often saw comets as warnings of disaster.

In 1910, Earth passed through the comet's tail. Newspapers reported that the tail contained a poisonous gas, and some sellers made money from "comet pills". The gas was far too thin to harm anyone. On its 1986 visit, the European probe Giotto flew past and photographed the comet's dark, peanut-shaped heart for the first time. Halley's will be back in 2061.

{{story:comets}}

Hale-Bopp was discovered in 1995 by two Americans, Alan Hale and Thomas Bopp, on the same night in different places. It was unusually big and bright. People could see it without a telescope for about 18 months, a record for modern times. In early 1997, millions of people in India, the USA and around the world watched it hang in the evening sky with two tails, one white and one blue.

Shoemaker-Levy 9 was found in 1993, already broken into a string of pieces like pearls on a necklace. Jupiter's strong gravity had torn it apart. In July 1994, more than 20 pieces crashed into the giant planet over six days. Each impact left dark marks in [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter's]] clouds, some larger than Earth.

It was the first time people had watched two objects in the solar system collide. It also showed how Jupiter's pull can capture and break up passing comets.

In 2014, the European Rosetta spacecraft reached comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko after a ten-year journey. It dropped a small lander, Philae, onto the surface. The lander bounced twice and ended up in a shadow, so its batteries soon ran out. Still, it was the first soft landing on a comet. Rosetta sent back photos of cliffs, boulders and jets of gas, from a comet shaped like a rubber duck.

Comet NEOWISE lit up the sky in July 2020, when many people were at home during lockdowns, and photographers in Ladakh and the USA captured it over mountains. Comet Tsuchinshan-ATLAS was easy to see in October 2024.

In 2025, astronomers spotted 3I/ATLAS, a comet coming from another star system. It was only the third such interstellar visitor ever found. It moved too fast to be caught by the Sun, so it will leave and never return.

Most comets come from two icy reservoirs: the [[@kuiper-belt|Kuiper Belt]] beyond Neptune and the much more distant Oort Cloud. Every year, sky-watchers discover dozens of new ones. Many leave behind trails of dust that Earth crosses, producing [[@shooting-stars|shooting stars]] on the same nights each year.

text: Sea cucumbers are soft, sausage-shaped animals that live on the seabed all over the world. Despite the name, they aren't plants. They are [[echinoderm|echinoderms]], the same animal family as [[@starfish|starfish]] and sea urchins. Like their cousins, they have tiny tube feet and a body built in five sections, though you have to look closely to see it.

There are more than 1,200 known kinds. Some are the size of your finger, while others grow to about 3 metres long. They crawl slowly across the sea floor, swallowing sand and mud and digesting the tiny bits of food inside. They live everywhere from shallow rock pools to the bottom of the deepest ocean trenches.

st.prompt: How does a sea cucumber get oxygen?

options.t: It pumps water in and out through its bottom
It gulps air at the surface like a whale
It has gills on its head like a fish

st.reveal: Many sea cucumbers breathe with branching tubes inside their body called respiratory trees. They suck water in through the anus, take oxygen from it, then squirt it back out the same way.

d.try: Watch how a sea cucumber stiffens. Fill a small plastic bag with cornflour and water mixed thick, like toothpaste, and seal it. Squeeze it fast and it feels firm. Press slowly and it goes soft and runny. Sea cucumbers can change their skin from firm to floppy in a similar way, though they use special proteins, not cornflour.
myth: Sea cucumbers are plants, like real cucumbers.
Sea cucumbers are animals. They eat, move, breathe and have babies. They're only named after cucumbers because of their long, lumpy shape.

sec.t:
A sea cucumber eats a bit like an [[@earthworms|earthworm]]. It shovels sand into its mouth with feathery tentacles, digests the bacteria, algae and dead scraps, and poos out cleaner sand. Over a year, that adds up. On one small reef in Australia's Great Barrier Reef, scientists estimated that sea cucumbers pass about 64,000 tonnes of sand through their bodies each year.

This churning keeps the seabed healthy. Their poo returns nutrients to the water, feeding algae and corals. It's also slightly alkaline, the opposite of acidic, which may help nearby [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]] cope with the sea becoming more acidic.

Sea cucumbers can't run, so they have unusual defences. When threatened, some species squirt out sticky white threads that tangle up crabs and fish. Others go further. They tear open their body wall and push out some of their guts. The attacker is distracted by the meal, and the sea cucumber crawls away. Over the next few weeks, it grows new organs.

Sea cucumbers can also change how stiff their skin is, in seconds. Special proteins let them go firm to resist an attack, or floppy enough to squeeze into a narrow crack in the rocks. Scientists are studying this trick for medical materials.

In the deep ocean, sea cucumbers are everywhere. On some parts of the dark abyssal plains, kilometres down, they make up most of the weight of all the animals living on the sea floor. Cameras lowered into deep trenches, more than 8 kilometres down, often find sea cucumbers crawling across the mud.

Some can even swim. A pinkish, see-through species nicknamed the "headless chicken monster" flaps its webbed skirt and rises off the seabed to drift to new feeding spots. Many deep-sea kinds glow with blue light when touched.

In parts of East and Southeast Asia, dried sea cucumber, called trepang or bêche-de-mer, is a prized and expensive delicacy. Centuries ago, sailors from Makassar in Indonesia sailed every year to northern Australia to collect sea cucumbers, trading with Aboriginal people there.

Heavy fishing has emptied many reefs. India banned catching all sea cucumbers in 2001, though smugglers still try to ship them abroad from the coasts of Tamil Nadu. Some even sell for more than fine meat, which is why they appear on lists of the world's [[@food-expensive|most expensive foods]].

text: An animal is [[endangered|endangered]] when so few are left that it could disappear for ever. Scientists at the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) keep a "Red List" that sorts species from *least concern* to *critically endangered* and finally *extinct*. More than 45,000 species on it are now threatened, from tigers and tortoises to frogs, sharks and trees.

There are a handful of big reasons. Forests and grasslands are cleared, so animals lose their homes, or [[habitat|habitat]]. Some are hunted or caught for trade. Pollution poisons rivers and food. Animals brought from elsewhere can eat or outcompete local ones. And a warming [[@climate-change|climate]] is shifting where many creatures can survive.

st.prompt: Across the world, what is the single biggest reason animals and plants become endangered?

options.t: Poaching for horns, tusks and skins
Losing the places where they live
Being eaten by other animals

st.reveal: Poaching is a serious danger for animals like rhinos and pangolins. But the biggest threat overall is habitat loss, when forests, grasslands and wetlands are turned into farms, roads, mines and towns. An animal with nowhere to live has nowhere to hide.

sec.t:
The great Indian bustard is a tall, heavy bird that walks the grasslands of Rajasthan and Gujarat. Fewer than about 150 remain, most in and around the Desert National Park near Jaisalmer. Grasslands look empty to many people, so they are often ploughed or covered with roads, [[@wind-turbines|wind farms]] and solar parks.

Bustards also have poor forward vision and fly into overhead power lines. Courts and conservationists have pushed for lines in key areas to be buried underground or marked so the birds can see them. Eggs are now being hatched in a breeding centre to build a backup flock.

Some stories turn around. By 1987 only 27 California condors were left, so American scientists caught every last one. They bred them in zoos and began releasing them in 1992. Today there are over 500, more than half of them flying free in California, Arizona, Utah and Mexico.

The [[@bald-eagle|bald eagle]], poisoned by the pesticide DDT, recovered after the chemical was banned in the USA in 1972. In India, one-horned [[@rhino-kaziranga|rhinos]] in Kaziranga, Assam, climbed from perhaps a few dozen in the early 1900s to more than 2,500.

Extinction is natural. Most species that ever lived died out long before humans existed. The difference today is speed. Species are vanishing many times faster than they did over most of Earth's history.

[[@lost-passenger-pigeon|The passenger pigeon]] shows how quickly it can happen. In the 1800s, flocks of billions crossed North America. Hunted for cheap meat and with their forests cut down, they crashed within a few decades. Martha, the last one, died at Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. Nobody had thought such a common bird could disappear. Its story helped push the USA to pass some of its first laws protecting wild birds. Today, Red List scientists hope to spot the next passenger pigeon while there is still time to act, and the list is how they keep watch.

text: Inside each earpiece of your headphones is a tiny loudspeaker, called a driver. It has a magnet, a coil of thin wire and a light, springy sheet called a diaphragm. Your phone sends an electrical signal that changes very fast, matching the shape of the music.

That signal flows through the coil, turning it into a little electromagnet. As the current flips back and forth, the coil is pushed and pulled by the fixed magnet, and it shakes the diaphragm. The diaphragm squeezes and stretches the air in front of it, making sound waves. Because your ear is only a centimetre or two away, a tiny movement is enough.

st.prompt: What actually makes the sound inside a headphone?

options.t: A thin sheet that a magnet pushes and pulls back and forth thousands of times a second
A tiny recording of a real orchestra
A small fan that blows air into your ear

st.reveal: Electric signals pass through a coil sitting near a magnet. The coil is pushed and pulled, and it shakes a thin diaphragm. That shaking pushes the air into sound waves, which travel the short way into your ear.

myth: If the music doesn't hurt, it can't damage your hearing.

Hearing damage often happens without any pain. Loud sound for long periods slowly harms tiny hair cells in the inner ear, and they don't grow back. Many doctors suggest keeping volume at or below about 60 percent, for no more than about 60 minutes at a time.

sec.t:
Early telephone operators used heavy single earpieces. Around 1910, Nathaniel Baldwin, an engineer in Utah, built a lighter, more sensitive pair at home and sent it to the US Navy. Navy radio operators needed to hear faint signals clearly, and the Navy ordered more.

For decades, headphones were tools for pilots, soldiers and radio workers. In 1958 an American company, Koss, sold stereo headphones made for listening to music. Then in 1979, Sony's Walkman cassette player let people carry music in their pockets. Suddenly headphones were everywhere: on buses in Tokyo, on Mumbai locals and on school buses in Ohio.

A [[@microphones|microphone]] works in almost exactly the opposite way. Sound waves shake a diaphragm, which moves a coil near a magnet, and that creates a small electrical signal. Engineers sometimes joke that a headphone is just a microphone that has learned to talk.

The same idea grows bigger in [[@loudspeakers|loudspeakers]] at concerts, which shake the air hard enough to feel in your chest.

Most headphones sold today are wireless. A tiny radio, using [[@bluetooth|Bluetooth]], receives music from your phone as digital code. A chip turns the code back into an electrical wave, and a small battery powers it all.

Noise-cancelling headphones go one step further. Little microphones listen to the noise around you, such as the rumble of a plane. A chip then creates the exact opposite wave and adds it to your music. When the two waves meet, they cancel out, a clever trick explained in [[@noise-cancelling|noise cancelling]].

Some headphones don't sit in your ear at all. Bone-conduction headphones rest on your cheekbones and shake your skull very slightly. The vibrations travel through bone straight to your inner ear. Runners like them because they can still hear traffic.

People have known about this for a long time. Stories say that [[@beethoven|Beethoven]], as he went deaf, held a rod between his teeth and pressed it against his piano to feel the notes.

The hair cells in your inner ear turn vibrations into nerve signals. Very loud sound can bend and damage them, and they do not grow back. In 2019 the World Health Organization warned that over a billion young people risked [[@hearing-loss|hearing loss]] from unsafe listening. Turning the volume down a notch, and taking breaks, protects ears you will need for the rest of your life.

text: When most things warm up, their tiny particles jiggle faster and push a little further apart, so the material grows. A classic thermometer uses this. It has a small bulb of liquid, usually coloured alcohol or, in older ones, mercury, joined to a very thin [[@glass-made|glass]] tube. As the liquid warms, it expands and has nowhere to go but up the tube. As it cools, it shrinks back down.

The tube is so narrow that a tiny change in the liquid shows as a big change in height. Marks printed beside the tube turn that height into a number of degrees. Digital thermometers do the same job with electricity instead of liquid.

st.prompt: A digital thermometer has no liquid inside it. What does it measure instead?

options.t: How easily electricity flows through a tiny part at its tip
How much light the skin gives off
How fast your heart beats

st.reveal: Most digital thermometers have a tiny part called a thermistor at the tip. Electricity flows through it more or less easily as it warms up. A chip measures that change and shows it as a temperature. Forehead and ear thermometers are different. They read invisible infrared light coming from your skin.

Push a clear straw in so it doesn't touch the bottom and seal the neck around it with modelling clay. Stand the bottle in a bowl of warm tap water and watch the coloured water creep up the straw. Move it to cold water and it sinks.
myth: Normal body temperature is exactly 37°C (98.6°F) for everyone.

Body temperature differs from person to person and changes through the day, usually lowest early in the morning. Anywhere from about 36°C to 37.5°C is common. That old 37°C figure is an average from the 1800s, and some recent studies suggest many people today run slightly cooler.

sec.t:
Around 1593, the Italian scientist [[@galileo|Galileo]] made a device called a thermoscope. It was a glass bulb with a long neck dipped into water. As the air in the bulb warmed or cooled, the water level in the neck went down or up. It showed that something was getting hotter, but it had no scale and was also affected by the weather.

Over the next century, people sealed the liquid inside the glass so air pressure couldn't change the reading. Then they needed a way to agree on the numbers. Early makers each chose their own marks, so a reading of 20 on one thermometer might mean something quite different on another. Scientists in different cities couldn't compare their results. The answer was to pick fixed points that anyone could check, such as melting ice and [[@boiling-water|boiling water]].

A digital thermometer has a small part at its tip called a thermistor. Electricity passes through it more easily, or less easily, as its temperature changes. A tiny chip measures the change and shows a number on the screen.

Forehead and ear thermometers work differently. Every warm object gives off invisible infrared light, and warmer things give off more. These thermometers catch that light without touching anything at all. During the COVID-19 pandemic, people met them at the doors of offices, shops and schools in India and the USA.

Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and it expands very evenly, which made it perfect for thermometers. But it is poisonous, and a broken thermometer leaves silvery beads that are hard to clean up. Many countries have now stopped selling mercury thermometers for home use. If one ever breaks at home, don't touch the beads or sweep them with a broom. Tell an adult, who can clean it up safely. Most home thermometers today are digital, or use harmless coloured alcohol, which is the red or blue line you often see.

Some special thermometers still measure the far ends of temperature. Weather stations record the heat that matters in [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]]. Laboratory thermometers measure things colder than the coldest Antarctic night, and others measure molten steel at more than 1,400°C.

text: Electronic music is music where the sounds are made or shaped by electricity. Older instruments rely on strings, drum skins or air in a tube. The main tool is the synthesizer. It builds a sound from an electric signal, which a [[@loudspeakers|loudspeaker]] then turns into vibrations in the air.
Today almost every song you hear has some electronic part, from a pop chorus to a Bollywood dance number. But it started a hundred years ago with odd machines that most people thought were toys.

st.reveal: A theremin senses how close your hands are to its two antennas. One hand changes the pitch and the other changes the volume, so you play it in mid-air.

People still choose every sound, rhythm and change. Many electronic musicians train for years, and plenty play keyboards, drum pads or controllers live on stage.

sec.t:
Around 1920 a Russian scientist called Leon Theremin built a box with two metal antennas. Moving one hand near the upright antenna raised or lowered the note. The other hand, near a loop, made it louder or softer. The sound was eerie and wobbly, like a singer humming through a pipe.

The theremin became the sound of flying saucers in 1950s science fiction films. It is hard to play well, because there are no keys or frets to tell you where a note is. Players learn to hold their fingers very still, since a tiny twitch bends the note out of tune. Clara Rockmore, a violinist who moved to the United States, became famous in the 1930s for playing classical pieces on it with real precision.

sec.h: Scissors, tape and a time machine
sec.t:
In the 1950s and 60s, people found they could make music by recording sounds on magnetic tape and then cutting, slowing down or looping it. In Britain, Delia Derbyshire of the BBC Radiophonic Workshop turned a written melody into the theme for *Doctor Who* in 1963. She built it note by note from tape, test-tone machines and careful splicing, without a synthesizer.

{{story:sound-recording}}

In 1964 the American engineer Robert Moog showed a synthesizer that musicians could play from a keyboard. Inside, electric circuits made simple waves. Knobs changed their shape and [[frequency|frequency]], which is how fast the wave wobbles and how high the note sounds. A smooth wave sounds soft, like a flute. A jagged one sounds buzzy, like a bee in a jar.

By the 1970s the German band Kraftwerk was making whole albums this way. Their robotic songs about trains and computers shaped pop, dance music and early [[@hip-hop|hip-hop]].

sec.h: A raga to a disco beat
sec.t:
In 1982 Charanjit Singh, a session musician who played for Hindi film recordings in Bombay, made an album called *Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat*. He used a Roland TB-303 bass machine, a drum machine and a synthesizer to play Indian ragas over a thumping beat.

Hardly anyone bought it. A few years later, musicians in Chicago used the same squelchy TB-303 sound to invent acid house. When the album was reissued in 2010, listeners were startled to hear that sound had already been tried in India.

Today a teenager with a laptop can do what once needed a room full of machines. Music software lets you record, loop and stack sounds on a screen. Producers also sample: they borrow a short clip of an old recording and build a new song around it.

Indian film music changed in the 1990s when composers like [[@ar-rahman|A.R. Rahman]] mixed synthesizers with folk singers, strings and tabla. Dance music festivals in Goa, Mumbai and Las Vegas now draw huge crowds, and the person on stage is often standing behind a table of glowing buttons.

Some of the newest tools even listen back. Drum machines can shuffle a beat slightly so it feels human, and software can tune a wobbly voice in an instant. Musicians still argue about how much of that is fair, which is the same argument people had about the first synthesizers sixty years ago.

text: India celebrates so many festivals because it holds so many different peoples, religions, languages and regions in one country. Each brings its own calendar of special days. Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, Jews and many tribal communities all have festivals of their own.

On top of religious days, there are harvest festivals tied to farming seasons, regional new years, and national days like Republic Day. Different states also use different calendars, some based on the Sun, some on the Moon and some on both. Put it all together, and there is hardly a month without a celebration somewhere in India.

st.prompt: Why does Eid fall about 11 days earlier each year on the usual calendar?

options.t: It follows a lunar calendar, which is shorter than the solar year
The government changes the date every year
It moves to avoid clashing with other festivals

st.reveal: The Islamic calendar has 12 lunar months, about 354 days. That's about 11 days shorter than the 365-day solar year, so Eid moves earlier each year and slowly passes through every season.

sec.h: Following the farm and the seasons
sec.t:
Many Indian festivals began as celebrations of farming. When a crop was harvested, there was food, rest and something to be thankful for.

In mid-January, as days start to lengthen, farmers in many states mark a winter harvest. In Tamil Nadu it is Pongal, when families cook rice with milk and jaggery until it boils over, a sign of plenty. In Punjab it is Lohri, with bonfires and songs. In Assam it is Magh Bihu, with feasts. In Gujarat it is Uttarayan, when the sky fills with kites, and in many states it is Makar Sankranti. In Kerala, the harvest festival is [[@onam-pongal|Onam]], in late summer.

Festivals jump around because India uses several calendars at once. The government's official dates follow the solar Gregorian calendar, like most of the world. But many Hindu festivals follow lunisolar calendars, which count months by the Moon but add an extra month every few years to keep in step with the seasons.

The Islamic calendar is purely lunar. Its year is about 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Eid moves earlier each year. Over about 33 years, it passes through every season. That's why Eid can fall in the heat of May one decade and the cool of winter another.

In many Indian cities and villages, festivals are shared. Neighbours bring sweets to each other at Diwali, Eid and Christmas. Schools often celebrate several festivals in one year. Durga Puja pandals in Kolkata draw visitors of every faith, and crowds of all backgrounds gather to see Christmas lights on Park Street.

Some temples, dargahs and gurdwaras welcome visitors of all religions. The langar, a free community meal at gurdwaras, feeds anyone who comes, whatever their background.

Festival times can also bring tensions, and disputes over processions or noise sometimes make the news. But for many Indians, celebrating each other's festivals is part of everyday life.

Three days belong to the whole country: Republic Day on 26 January, Independence Day on 15 August and Gandhi Jayanti on 2 October. They are celebrated by everyone, with flag hoisting, parades and school events.

On Republic Day, a grand parade moves along Kartavya Path in New Delhi. Floats from different states show off their dances, crafts and festivals. In a single morning, you can see how many traditions fit inside one country.

text: Area tells you how much flat surface something covers, like the floor of your classroom. You measure it by counting how many squares of a set size would cover it, such as square centimetres (cm²) or square metres (m²). For a rectangle, you multiply length by width.

Volume tells you how much space something takes up, or how much it can hold, like a water tank. You measure it in cubes, such as cubic centimetres (cm³) or cubic metres (m³). For a box, you multiply length by width by height. A cube 10 cm on each side holds exactly 1 litre.

st.prompt: A square tile has sides of 10 cm. A bigger tile has sides of 20 cm. How many small tiles would cover the big one?
st.reveal: Doubling the side doubles both the length and the width, so the area grows 2 × 2 = 4 times. If they were cubes, the bigger one would hold 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 small cubes.

d.try: Fill a small box, like a matchbox or a juice carton, with water or dry rice. Measure its length, width and height in centimetres and multiply them. Then pour the contents into a measuring jug. Is the number of millilitres close to your answer? It should be, because 1 cm³ is 1 ml.
myth: Archimedes shouted "Eureka" and ran naked through the streets after discovering how to measure volume in his bath.

The story was written down by the Roman writer Vitruvius about 200 years after Archimedes lived, and may be a legend. Archimedes certainly understood how objects push aside water, but nobody knows if the bath scene really happened.

sec.t:
Suppose your bedroom floor is 4 m long and 3 m wide. Picture square tiles, each 1 m by 1 m. You could fit 4 in a row, and 3 rows, so 12 tiles. The area is 12 m².

Not every shape is a rectangle. A triangle covers half the area of the rectangle drawn around it, so its area is half the base times the height. A circle's area is π times the radius times the radius. That is where [[@pi|pi]], about 3.14, comes in.

Land is often measured in bigger units. A hectare is 10,000 m², a square 100 m on each side. In India, many people buy and sell land in older local units too, like the *bigha* or *gaj* (a square yard). A bigha varies from state to state, so two families in [[@villages-india|villages]] in different states might mean quite different sizes by the same word.

How do you find the volume of a stone, a toy or your own hand? You can't multiply length by width by height. But you can drop it into water. The water level rises by exactly the volume of the object, because the object pushes that much water out of the way.

The Greek thinker Archimedes understood this more than 2,000 years ago. He also worked out why objects [[@floating-ships|float]]: a floating ship pushes aside water that weighs as much as the whole ship.

Here is a surprising rule. If you double every length of a shape, its area grows four times, but its volume grows eight times. Make it ten times bigger and the area grows 100 times, but the volume 1,000 times.

This explains a lot about living things. An animal's weight depends on its volume, but the strength of its bones and legs depends on their cross-section, which is an area. So a giant animal needs very thick legs. That is why an [[@elephants-talk|elephant]] has legs like pillars, while a mouse can have thin ones. It is also why a [[@big-small-scale|giant insect]] the size of a car, from a science-fiction film, would collapse under its own weight.

text: Bhaskara II, also called Bhaskaracharya, was one of medieval India's greatest mathematicians and astronomers. Born in 1114 CE, he became head of the astronomical observatory at Ujjain, a famous centre of learning where [[@brahmagupta|Brahmagupta]] had worked five centuries earlier.

Around 1150 he finished a huge work called the Siddhanta Shiromani, the "crown jewel of astronomy". Its first part, the Lilavati, teaches arithmetic through puzzles written as poems. Its second, the Bijaganita, covers [[@algebra|algebra]]. Together they were copied, studied and taught across India for centuries.

st.prompt: Bhaskara II wrote about what happens when you divide a number by zero. What did he say the answer was?

options.t: An endless quantity that doesn't change if you add to it
Zero
The number you started with

st.reveal: He called it khahara and described it as infinite, unchanged by adding or taking away. Modern maths says division by zero is undefined instead, but his idea shows him thinking hard about infinity.

Bhaskara wrote that the Earth has a natural power of attraction that pulls heavy things towards it, building on older Indian ideas. But he didn't give a mathematical law for how gravity works across space. That came from Newton in 1687.

sec.t:
The Lilavati speaks to a young reader, often addressed as a clever girl, and sets problems about everyday things. There are questions about bees among flowers, a peacock pouncing on a snake, the price of goods in a market and the size of a bamboo broken by the wind.

Each problem is a short verse in Sanskrit, so students could learn it by heart. Working out the answer meant using rules for fractions, [[@square-roots|square roots]], interest, areas and volumes. That mix of story and maths kept the book popular. In 1587, the poet Faizi translated it into Persian for the Mughal emperor [[@akbar|Akbar]].

A much-told legend says Bhaskara named the book after his daughter, Lilavati. The story comes from long after his death and may not be true, but it has made the book even more famous.

{{story:akbar}}

Bhaskara wrote clear rules for working with [[@zero-invent|zero]]. Adding zero changes nothing. Multiplying by zero gives zero. Then he tackled the hard case: dividing by zero.

He called the result khahara, which means "with zero as its divisor", and described it as an endless quantity. Adding to it or taking away from it, he wrote, makes no difference, just as the infinite god Vishnu is unchanged by the worlds that come and go. Mathematicians today say dividing by zero has no answer at all, but Bhaskara's thinking shows how seriously he took the puzzle of [[@infinity|infinity]].

In the Bijaganita, Bhaskara solved problems where you hunt for whole numbers that fit [[@equations|equations]] like 61 × y² + 1 = x². The smallest answer is huge: x is 1,766,319,049 and y is 226,153,980.

He used a step-by-step method called chakravala, meaning "wheel", which improved on ideas from Brahmagupta and the later scholar Jayadeva. In 1657, Fermat set this exact equation as a challenge to other European mathematicians. Europe worked out a full general method only in the 1700s.

The later parts of the Siddhanta Shiromani deal with the movements of planets, [[@eclipses|eclipses]], and the shape of the Earth. Bhaskara explained that the Earth is a sphere hanging in space, held in place by its own power, and that it attracts heavy objects towards itself.

Some people today say this means he discovered gravity before [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]]. Historians are more careful. Bhaskara's idea was a description, not a law with a formula that explains orbits and tides. Even so, his astronomy tables were accurate enough to be used for [[@calendars|calendars]] for centuries.

In 1207, Bhaskara's grandson set up a school to study his works, recorded in a stone inscription in Maharashtra. Today his books are still read in their original Sanskrit and in translation, and his puzzles still turn up in Indian textbooks.

text: A wheel turns around an axle, a rod through its middle. On a circle, every point on the edge is exactly the same distance from the centre. That distance is called the [[radius|radius]].
So as a round wheel rolls, the axle stays at the same height above the road the whole time. The cart, car or bicycle glides along without bouncing.

Try that with a square wheel. Its corners are further from the centre than the middle of its sides. As it turns, the axle would rise onto each corner, then drop again, thump, thump, thump. Every other flat-sided shape has the same problem, only smaller.

st.prompt: Why are most manhole covers round instead of square?

options.t: A round cover can't fall down through its own hole
Round covers are cheaper to paint
Square covers are against the law

st.reveal: A circle is the same width in every direction, so there is no way to tip a round cover through its hole. A square cover can slip through if you turn it on its side, because its diagonal is longer than its sides.

d.try: Lay two round pencils on a table and rest a book on them. Push the book and it rolls smoothly. Now try the same with two pencils that have six flat sides, or with a few square erasers. Notice how the book bumps up and down when the rollers aren't round.
myth: A circle is the only shape that rolls with the same width all the way round.

Many shapes have this "constant width". The simplest after the circle is the Reuleaux triangle, a triangle with bulging sides. It rolls smoothly between two flat boards, but its centre wobbles, so it can't spin on an axle.

sec.h: The magic number inside every circle
sec.t:
Measure the distance around any circle, then measure straight across it. The first number is always about 3.14 times the second. This number is called [[@pi|pi]], and it is the same for a bangle, a bicycle wheel or the rim of a stadium.

That means one turn of a wheel moves it forward about 3.14 times its own width. A bicycle wheel about 70 cm across travels roughly 2.2 metres every time it goes round. A bicycle's computer uses exactly this idea to count your distance from how many times the wheel turns.

Here is something that surprises even grown-ups. Draw an equal-sided triangle. Now, with a compass point on each corner in turn, draw a curve joining the other two corners. You get a fat, rounded triangle called a Reuleaux triangle, after a German engineer, Franz Reuleaux, who studied it in the 1800s.

It has the same width whichever way you measure it. Lay a board on top of a few of them and it rolls along perfectly flat. The British 20p and 50p coins use a seven-sided version of the same idea, which helps [[@vending-machines|vending machines]] measure them.

So why not use them as wheels? Because the centre of a Reuleaux triangle moves up and down as it rolls. You can't fix an axle to it. Only a circle keeps its centre still.

{{story:wheel-invented}}

Wheels seem obvious now, but people lived for a very long time without them. Wheeled carts appear in the Middle East and Europe a little over 5,000 years ago. The oldest wooden wheel yet found, from the Ljubljana Marshes in Slovenia, is about 5,000 years old.

In the [[@indus-cities|Indus Valley cities]] of what is now Pakistan and north-west India, archaeologists have dug up little clay toy carts with round wheels, made about 4,500 years ago. Children were pushing them around long before anyone wrote a book about geometry.

A wheel needs more than a round shape, though. It needs a smooth axle, a strong hole in the middle and a road that isn't too rough. Getting all of those right at once is part of why the [[@wheel-invented|wheel took so long]] to appear.

Round shapes are good at more than rolling. A circle encloses the most space for a given length of edge, which is why water tanks, pipes and [[@canned-food|cans]] are often round. A round pipe also spreads the push of the water inside evenly in every direction, so there are no weak corners to burst.

And then there are manhole covers. Because a circle is the same width all the way round, a round cover can never be tipped down its own hole, however you turn it.

text: When you count to ten, you run out of single digits and start again, putting a 1 in the tens place. This is called base ten, or the decimal system. Almost every culture on Earth counts in tens, and the simplest explanation is right at the end of your arms. People counted on their [[@maths-binary-fingers|fingers]] long before they wrote numbers down.

But tens are not the only choice. Some peoples counted in twenties, using fingers and toes. Others used fives, eights, [[@clocks-maths|twelves]] or sixties. Computers count in twos. Traces of these other systems hide in our clocks, our languages and even in [[@speeches-famous|famous speeches]].

st.prompt: In French, the number 80 is said as quatre-vingts. What does that mean word for word?

options.t: Four twenties
Eight tens
Two forties

st.reveal: Quatre means four and vingt means twenty. It is a leftover from an older way of counting in twenties. English has one too. A "score" is 20, so "four score and seven" means 87.

src: Ifrah G. (2000) The Universal History of Numbers. Wiley.
Britannica, "Numerals and numeral systems".
n.certNote: Nearly all historians agree that fingers explain why base ten is so common, but nobody can prove it, since counting began long before writing.

d.try: Count a big handful of dried beans or buttons in fives instead of tens. Make piles of five, then group five piles together into a "big pile" of 25. Write your answer as big piles, piles and loose beans. You have just written a number in base five.
myth: Base ten is the most natural and best way to count.

It is the most common because of our fingers, but mathematicians point out that 12 can be divided evenly by 2, 3, 4 and 6, while 10 only splits neatly into 2 and 5. That is one reason dozens, 12-inch feet and 24-hour days have lasted so long.

sec.h: Ten digits and a clever trick
sec.t:
The digits we use, 0 to 9, plus the idea that a digit's place shows its value, were developed in India. In 222, the first 2 means two hundreds, the second two tens and the last just two. With [[@zero-invent|zero]] as a placeholder, ten symbols can write any number at all.

Arab scholars learned this system and carried it west. Europeans called the digits Arabic numerals, but Arab writers called them Indian numbers. Today they are often called Hindu-Arabic numerals. They replaced clumsy systems like [[@roman-numerals|Roman numerals]], because they make sums much faster.

The digits did not always look the way they do now. Early Indian forms of the numbers, found in inscriptions and old manuscripts, changed shape as they travelled. The 2 and 3 you write probably began as two and three short strokes, joined together by fast-moving pens. Even today, the Devanagari digits used in Hindi look quite different from the ones in this sentence.

The Maya of Central America counted in twenties, perhaps using fingers and toes. They had a symbol for zero and wrote numbers with dots, bars and a shell shape. The [[@aztecs-maya|Maya]] used this system to run detailed [[@calendars|calendars]].

Twenty also left marks in Europe. In French, 80 is quatre-vingts, "four twenties". Old English counted in scores, or twenties. When [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] began his Gettysburg Address in 1863 with "Four score and seven years ago", he meant 87 years.

Some peoples counted in eights. The Yuki of California are said to have counted the spaces between their fingers instead of the fingers themselves. Number words around the world show huge variety, as you can see in the many [[@languages-world|languages of the world]].

{{story:languages-world}}

The Babylonians, about 4,000 years ago, counted in sixties. We still use their system for time and angles: 60 seconds, 60 minutes and 360 degrees. Sixty can be split evenly in many ways, which helps when dividing things up.

Twelve shows up a lot too. There are 12 months, 12 hours on a clock face, 12 inches in a foot and 12 items in a dozen. A few enthusiasts even argue the world should switch to base 12, because 12 divides more neatly than 10. They call it dozenal counting.

Computers use base two, called [[@binary-code|binary]]. A tiny switch is either off or on, so it can show only 0 or 1. In binary, 2 is written 10, 4 is 100 and 8 is 1000. Programmers also use base 16, called hexadecimal, using the letters A to F for the numbers 10 to 15.

Even within base ten, people group digits differently. Indians write one hundred thousand as 1,00,000, a lakh, and ten million as 1,00,00,000, a crore. Americans write 100,000 and 10,000,000. The digits are the same; only the commas move.

myth: Sitting close to the TV will permanently damage your eyes.

Eye doctors say there is no good evidence that sitting close harms your eyes for good. Long hours of screen time can make eyes tired and dry, so it helps to take breaks and look into the distance. If your eyes hurt or you struggle to see, tell a parent or see an eye doctor.

sec.t:
India's TV began on 15 September 1959, as an experiment by [[@radio-india|All India Radio]] in Delhi. It broadcast for about an hour, a couple of days a week, mostly educational programmes for schools and community groups. Very few people owned a set, so many sets were placed in schools and community halls.

Daily broadcasts began in 1965. In 1967, *Krishi Darshan* started teaching farmers near Delhi about seeds, fertilisers and new methods, during the years of the [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]]. In 1976, TV was separated from radio and became Doordarshan, which means "seeing far" in Hindi.

Colour TV arrived in 1982, just before the [[@asian-games|Asian Games]] in Delhi. A colour picture mixes red, green and blue light in different amounts, as explained in [[@colour-mix|colour mixing]]. Sales of TV sets shot up.

The 1980s brought shows that the whole country watched together. *Hum Log*, India's first soap opera, began in 1984. When *Ramayan* was broadcast on Sunday mornings in 1987 and 1988, many streets emptied as families gathered around TVs. Some people garlanded their TV sets. The [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] had been told for thousands of years, and now crores watched it at the same moment.

In the early 1990s, private [[@satellite-tv|satellite channels]] arrived, beamed from abroad. People put dish antennas on rooftops, and cable operators ran wires from building to building. Within a few years, viewers had dozens of channels, including news, music and cartoons all day.

Indian children's shows grew too. *[[@malgudi|Malgudi Days]]*, based on [[@stories-last|R.K. Narayan's stories]], began in 1986, and the superhero show *Shaktimaan* started in 1997.

A TV camera turns a scene into an electrical signal, line by line. A transmitter on a tall tower sends that signal out as [[@radio-waves|radio waves]], and an antenna on a roof catches it. A satellite works like a very tall tower, about 36,000 km up, so one satellite can reach a whole country. Old TV sets then fired beams at the screen to light up coloured dots, row after row, many times a second.

In the USA, regular TV broadcasts began around 1939, two decades before India. Colour TV started there in the 1950s. In 1969, hundreds of millions of people around the world watched live pictures of astronauts walking on the Moon.

Today India has hundreds of TV channels, in dozens of languages. Many people now watch shows on phones, through the internet, whenever they like. But big cricket matches still bring families together around one screen, just as the first Doordarshan broadcasts did.

text: Water is heavy. As you go down, more and more of it presses on you from above. Every 10 metres of sea water adds about the same push as the whole [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] above us. So at 10 metres, the pressure is double; at 20 metres, triple.

Your body is mostly water, which hardly squashes. But air does. The air in your lungs, ears, sinuses and even a diving mask gets squeezed into a smaller space as you sink. That is why your ears hurt at the bottom of a deep pool. Divers must manage this squeeze, along with cold, darkness and the risk of bubbles forming in their blood on the way up.

st.reveal: At 10 metres, the pressure is about double that at the surface. The air inside the balloon gets squeezed into roughly half the space. The air in a diver's lungs and ears is squeezed the same way.

sec.t:
The first thing most swimmers notice is pain in their ears. Behind each eardrum is a small pocket of air. As water [[pressure|pressure]] rises, it pushes the eardrum inward. Divers fix this by "equalising": pinching their nose and gently blowing, or swallowing, to push air up a narrow tube from the throat into the middle ear.

It is the same trick that helps on a plane coming in to land. Divers equalise often on the way down, before it hurts. Forcing it or diving with a blocked nose from a cold can damage the [[@ears-hear|ears]].

People have dived for food and treasure for thousands of years. In the Gulf of Mannar, between India and Sri Lanka, divers once collected [[@pearls|pearls]] from oyster beds on a single breath. In Japan and Korea, women divers called ama and haenyeo still gather shellfish and seaweed, some well into their seventies.

The Bajau, a sea-going people in Indonesia, the Philippines and Malaysia, spend hours a day in the water. A 2018 study found that their spleens are much larger than those of nearby farming people. The spleen stores red blood cells and squeezes them into the blood during a dive, giving an extra boost of oxygen.

Breathing compressed air from a tank lets a scuba diver stay down much longer. But under pressure, extra nitrogen from the air dissolves into the blood and body tissues, like gas in a sealed bottle of soda. If the diver rises too fast, the pressure drops and the nitrogen forms bubbles, just as when the soda is opened.

Those bubbles can cause pain in the joints, dizziness and worse. This is decompression sickness, or the bends. It became famous in the 1870s among workers digging foundations for the Brooklyn Bridge in New York, who worked in pressurised chambers under the river and then came up too quickly. Today, divers follow tables or dive computers that tell them how slowly to rise, sometimes pausing on the way up.

Below about 40 metres, breathing ordinary air can make divers feel drunk and confused, an effect called nitrogen narcosis. Deeper still, special gas mixtures are needed. At the bottom of the Mariana Trench, almost 11 km down, the pressure is more than 1,000 times that at the surface.

Only a few people have been there, sealed inside thick metal [[@submarines|submarines]] built to resist the crush. The first were Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh in 1960. Their dive to the bottom took almost five hours.

text: A microscope uses lenses to bend light so that tiny things look much bigger. Before microscopes, nobody knew that a drop of water could be crowded with living creatures. Nobody knew that blood is made of separate cells, or that germs too small to see could cause disease.

The first microscopes appeared in the [[@amsterdam|Netherlands]] around 1600, made by [[@eyesight-glasses|spectacle makers]] who found that stacking [[@lenses-glasses|lenses]] could magnify things. In the 1660s and 1670s, two men used microscopes to open up a hidden world: Robert Hooke in England and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in the Netherlands. Later, electron microscopes let scientists see things thousands of times smaller still.

Inside a diamond

st.reveal: Leeuwenhoek scraped a little plaque from his teeth, mixed it with water and looked through his lens. He described many tiny "animalcules" moving about. His drawings are among the first records of bacteria.

Look through the drop. The curved water bends light like a lens and makes the letters look bigger. Try different drop sizes.
myth: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek invented the microscope.

Microscopes existed before him, made by lens makers in the Netherlands around 1600. Leeuwenhoek made far better ones than anybody else in his time, and he was the first to see and describe bacteria and many other tiny living things.

sec.t:
Robert Hooke was a brilliant English scientist who built a compound microscope, one with more than one lens. In 1665 he published a book called Micrographia, filled with large, detailed drawings of what he saw.

One showed a flea, drawn so big it folded out of the book, its armoured body and hairy legs shocking to readers. Another showed a thin slice of cork. Hooke saw it was made of tiny empty boxes and called them "cells". He was looking at the walls of dead plant cells, the first [[@body-cells|cells]] anyone had described. The word stuck.

For almost two centuries, the tiny creatures were treated mostly as curiosities. Then, in the 1800s, better microscopes helped scientists such as Louis Pasteur in France and Robert Koch in Germany show that [[@disease-history|particular microbes cause particular diseases]]. Koch identified the bacteria behind [[@tb-india|tuberculosis]] in 1882. In 1884 he announced the cause of cholera, after studying patients in Egypt and in Calcutta.

This led to washing hands, cleaner [[@hospitals|hospitals]], safer water and [[@vaccines|vaccines]]. Most microbes, it turned out, are harmless or even helpful. But the dangerous ones could now be seen, studied and fought.

Ordinary light microscopes have a limit. Light waves are too large to show things smaller than about a fifth of a thousandth of a millimetre. Viruses and the fine details inside cells stay blurry.

In 1931, the German engineers Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built the first electron microscope, which uses beams of electrons instead of light. Electrons behave like waves far shorter than light, so they can show much finer detail. Modern electron microscopes can show individual atoms. Ruska shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.

Microscopes used to be too expensive for many schools. In 2014, Manu Prakash, an Indian-born scientist at Stanford University, and his team introduced the Foldscope, a microscope folded from a sheet of printed card with a tiny lens. It costs less than a dollar to make in parts and can magnify about 140 times. Children and health workers in India and many other countries have used Foldscopes to look at insects, pollen and pond life.

text: Sound is a wave of air pressure: tiny squeezes and stretches of air rushing towards your ear. Noise-cancelling [[@sound-recording|headphones]] have small [[@microphones|microphones]] that listen to the noise around you. A chip inside works out the exact opposite wave, with a stretch wherever the noise has a squeeze, and plays it through the [[@loudspeakers|speaker]].

When the two waves meet, they cancel each other out, and you hear much less noise. This is called destructive interference. It works best on low, steady sounds like the drone of a plane engine, the hum of an air conditioner or the rumble of a Mumbai local train.

st.reveal: Low, steady sounds are easy for the headphones to predict and cancel. Sudden, high-pitched sounds change too quickly, so the headphones rely more on their cushions to muffle those.

d.try: Fill a wide tray or basin with a few centimetres of water. Tap the water gently with one finger at each end at the same moment and watch the ripples meet in the middle. In some places the ripples add up, and in others they flatten out. Those flat spots are what noise-cancelling does to sound.
myth: Noise-cancelling headphones block sound just by having thick padding.

Padding helps, especially with high-pitched sounds, but the main trick is electronic. Tiny microphones listen to the noise, and a chip plays an opposite sound wave that cancels much of it before it reaches your ear.

sec.t:
To cancel noise, the headphones have to react extremely quickly. A microphone on the outside hears noise coming. Another inside the ear cup checks what's actually reaching your ear. The chip compares them and adjusts the anti-noise thousands of times a second.

Low sounds have long, slow waves, which are easier to predict and match. High sounds have short, fast waves, and voices and clatter change suddenly. So electronics handle the low rumble, and the cushions and ear tips do the rest by blocking higher sounds, a method called passive isolation. Together they cut a lot of noise, but never all of it.

sec.h: From an old patent to the cockpit
sec.t:
In the 1930s a German physicist, Paul Lueg, patented the idea of cancelling sound with an opposite sound wave. But the electronics of his time were too slow and bulky to make it practical.

The idea took off with pilots. In 1978 the American engineer Amar Bose, founder of the Bose company, was on a flight and found his headphones useless against the cabin noise. He started working on noise-cancelling headsets. In 1986 the pilots Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager flew the Voyager aircraft non-stop around the world in nine days without refuelling. They wore early noise-cancelling headsets to protect their ears from the engine roar. Pilots and [[@airplanes-fly|aircraft]] crews were the first big users.

Loud noise over time damages the tiny hair cells in your [[@ears-hear|inner ear]], and they don't grow back. This can lead to [[@hearing-loss|hearing loss]]. On a noisy bus or plane, people often turn their music up very loud to drown out the background. With noise cancelling, they can hear clearly at a lower, safer volume. The World Health Organization suggests keeping volume low and taking listening breaks.

There's a safety side too. Blocking out sound can make people miss car horns, bicycle bells or announcements. Many headphones now have a "transparency" mode that uses the outside microphones to let important sounds back in.

The same idea is used beyond headphones. Many phones use extra microphones to cancel background noise during calls, so your friend hears [[@voice|your voice]] and not the traffic. Some cars cancel engine boom inside the cabin through the speakers. Engineers are also testing it in [[@soundproofing|quiet rooms]], air vents and even windows, though cancelling sound across a whole space is much harder than inside a small ear cup.

text: The Chenab Rail Bridge crosses a deep Himalayan gorge in the Reasi district of Jammu and Kashmir. Its deck stands 359 metres above the river. That is about 30 metres higher than the tip of the Eiffel Tower, and as tall as a 120-storey building. It is the highest railway arch bridge in the world.

Engineers built it from about 28,000 tonnes of steel. The great arch spans 467 metres in a single leap, with no support in the middle. Building it took years of work on steep, crumbling slopes, with giant cable cranes, careful rock studies and a lot of patience.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi opened it on 6 June 2025. Vande Bharat trains now run across it between Katra and Srinagar.

options.t: With giant cable cranes strung between the two sides
With helicopters carrying every piece
By floating parts up the river on boats

st.reveal: Two cable cranes were stretched across the valley between tall towers on each bank. Like a ropeway, they carried steel sections out over the gorge and lowered them into place.

d.try: Make an arch from a strip of thin card bent between two stacks of books. Press gently on top, then add a small weight. Now try a flat strip of card with no arch. Notice how the arch pushes into the books and holds far more.
myth: An arch bridge is weakest at the top of its curve, so it needs pillars in the middle.
A well-built arch turns weight into a squeeze that flows down both sides into the ground. The Chenab arch carries its trains across 467 metres without any pillar standing in the river.
facts: winds of about 260 km/h and strong earthquakes

sec.t:
For more than a century, the Kashmir Valley had no railway link to the rest of India. Roads over the mountains could close for days in winter because of snow and landslides. The bridge is part of a long rail line that winds through 36 main tunnels and hundreds of bridges to connect the valley.

The Chenab gorge was the hardest gap of all. The river runs at the bottom of a deep, narrow valley. Building tall piers down there would have been slow and risky, so the engineers chose an [[@bridges|arch]] instead. An arch pushes its weight sideways and down into the rock on each side of the gorge, like a person bracing their arms against a doorway.

Work began in 2004, but stopped in 2008 over worries about the steep slopes and strong winds. Engineers from India and abroad, including experts from IISc Bengaluru, studied the rock again. Work restarted in 2010 with stronger foundations and slopes held in place by anchors and concrete.

To build the arch, two cable cranes were strung between tall towers on both sides of the valley. They worked like a giant ropeway, carrying steel pieces out over empty air. The arch grew outward from each bank at the same time. Each half was tied back with steel cables so it wouldn't fall while it was still incomplete.

In April 2021 the two halves finally met in the middle, high above the river. Workers called the last piece the "golden joint".

{{story:indian-railways}}

sec.h: Ready for wind, quakes and cold
sec.t:
The Himalaya is still rising, and this region has strong [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]]. The bridge was designed to survive the most severe kind of shaking expected in the area. It can also stand up to winds of about 260 km/h, faster than the strongest cyclone gusts most coastal cities ever see.

Sensors on the bridge watch the wind all the time. If gusts get too strong, signals stop trains from crossing until it calms down. The arch is made of hollow steel boxes, and some were filled with concrete to make it heavier and steadier in the wind.

Winter temperatures here can fall well below freezing. Steel shrinks in cold and stretches in heat, so the bridge has joints that let it move a little without cracking. It is designed to last about 120 years.

The [[@eiffel-tower|Eiffel Tower]] is about 330 metres tall to its tip. Stand it on the riverbed under the Chenab Bridge and a train would still pass about 30 metres above its top.

For people who live nearby, the bridge means faster, safer journeys in every season. For visitors, the view from a train window is dizzying. The river looks like a thin blue-green ribbon far below. The [[@vande-bharat|Vande Bharat]] trains on this route were also adapted for the cold, with heated windscreens and pipes that don't freeze.

And the strangest part? India's longest railway tunnel in the Himalaya lies on this same line, part of a whole family of record-breaking spans and tunnels you can explore in [[@extreme-longest-bridges|the world's longest bridges]].

text: The Mahabharata is an ancient Indian [[epic|epic]] in [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]]. At its heart is a family quarrel. Two groups of cousins, the five Pandava brothers and the hundred Kauravas, fight over the kingdom of Hastinapura. Tricked out of their share in a game of dice, the Pandavas spend 13 years in exile. Talks fail, and the cousins meet in a great war on the field of Kurukshetra, which lasts 18 days.

The epic is traditionally said to have been composed by the sage Vyasa. With about 100,000 verses in its longest versions, it is several times longer than the Greek *Iliad* and *Odyssey* put together.

st.reveal: The war lasts 18 days. The number 18 runs through the epic. It has 18 books, and the Bhagavad Gita has 18 chapters.

Then talk with a family member about whether the choice was right. You may not agree, and the epic doesn't always settle it either.
myth: The Bhagavad Gita is a separate book from the Mahabharata.
The Gita is part of the Mahabharata, found in its sixth book, the Bhishma Parva. It is often printed and read on its own, which is why many people think of it as separate.
facts: about 100,000 verses in its longest versions

sec.t:
The Mahabharata is built like a set of nested boxes. Storytellers tell other storytellers what they heard. The main tale is also full of side stories. There is the love of Nala and Damayanti, the clever Savitri who argues with the god of death, and even a short version of the Ramayana.

Its characters are rarely simply good or bad. Arjuna is a great archer who doubts himself. Karna, a brave warrior raised by a charioteer, learns only shortly before the war that he is the Pandavas' elder brother. Draupadi, married to all five Pandavas, demands justice when she is insulted in the royal court. The epic asks hard questions about duty, loyalty and fairness, and it doesn't always give easy answers.

A much-loved legend says Vyasa needed a scribe fast enough to keep up. The elephant-headed god [[@myths-ganesha-stories|Ganesha]] agreed, on one condition: Vyasa must never stop reciting. Vyasa added his own condition: Ganesha must understand every verse before writing it down. Whenever Vyasa needed a rest, he composed a tricky verse to keep Ganesha thinking.

Historians tell a different kind of story. The epic was probably passed on by storytellers for centuries, growing as it went, and written down in many versions. Between 1919 and 1966, scholars at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune compared more than a thousand manuscripts to produce a "critical edition", their best estimate of the oldest shared text.

The Mahabharata is everywhere in Indian life. [[@indian-classical-dance|Kathakali]] dancers in [[@kerala|Kerala]] perform its battles with painted faces and huge skirts. People still call a trap you can enter but not escape a *chakravyuha*, after a battle formation in the epic. Comics such as [[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]] introduced millions of children to its heroes.

In 1988, B. R. Chopra's TV series began on Doordarshan, and like the Ramayan series before it, it emptied streets on Sunday mornings. Abroad, the British director Peter Brook staged a nine-hour play of the epic in 1985. Its questions about family, power and right action still feel surprisingly modern.

text: The ancient Maya believed the world had layers. Above were 13 levels of heaven. In the middle was the Earth, where people lived. Below were 9 levels of a dark underworld called Xibalba, "the place of fear".

At the centre of everything stood a giant world tree, often shown as a ceiba tree, linking the heavens, the Earth and the underworld. The Maya believed gods controlled rain, maize, the Sun and the Moon, and that people had to honour them to keep the world running. They told these beliefs in stories, painted them on pots and carved them in stone.

st.reveal: The twins Hunahpu and Xbalanque survive deadly tests set by the lords of Xibalba using cleverness. They play the sacred ball game, pass through dangerous houses, and finally trick the lords into their own defeat.

myth: The Maya predicted that the world would end in 2012.

A cycle of the Maya Long Count calendar ended in December 2012, like a car's odometer rolling over. Maya writings never said the world would end. Some inscriptions even mention dates thousands of years after 2012.

sec.t:
The most famous Maya stories come from the Popol Vuh, the sacred book of the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala. It begins with the gods in a quiet, dark sea, deciding to make the world.

They wanted beings who would speak and remember them. First they made people of mud. These crumbled and dissolved in water. Next they carved people of wood. These could talk, but had no hearts or minds, and forgot their makers. A great flood swept them away. Some survivors, the story says, became monkeys.

Finally, the gods ground yellow and white [[@corn-maize|maize]] into dough and shaped the first true humans. Maize was the Maya's most important food, so this story made people and their crop part of the same family.

The longest part of the Popol Vuh tells of the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque. Their father and uncle had been tricked and killed by the lords of Xibalba after a noisy ball game disturbed the underworld.

The twins went down to face the same lords. They passed through the House of Gloom, the House of Knives, the House of Cold, the House of Jaguars and the House of Bats. Each time, they survived through tricks.

In the end, the twins pretended to perform a magic act. The lords were so impressed that they asked to try it themselves, and the twins defeated them. The brothers then rose into the sky as the Sun and the Moon.

{{story:zero-invent}}

The Maya ball game was more than a sport. Players had to keep a heavy rubber ball in the air using hips, thighs and arms, not hands. Stone courts were built in many cities, some with rings high on the walls.

The game echoed the twins' story, the movement of the Sun and the battle between life and death. Rubber balls, made from the sap of local trees, were in use in the region thousands of years before Europeans had ever seen rubber.

sec.h: Time that goes round and round
sec.t:
The Maya were brilliant at tracking time. They used several [[@calendars|calendars]] at once. One had 260 days, another had 365. Together they made a cycle of 52 years.

For longer periods, they used the Long Count, which counted days from a starting date in 3114 BCE. To write it, they needed a symbol for nothing, so they used [[@zero-invent|zero]], shown as a shell. They were among the first peoples in the world to use zero, centuries before it reached Europe from India.

The Maya saw time as cycles that repeat, like seasons. That is why the end of one Long Count cycle in 2012 did not mean the end of the world, only the start of a new count.

Spanish soldiers arrived in the 1500s. Priests burned many Maya books, and only four are known to survive today. The Popol Vuh survived because Maya writers wrote it down in the Latin alphabet in the 1550s. Around 1701, a Spanish priest, Francisco Ximénez, copied it, and that copy is the one we read.

Today, millions of Maya people live in Mexico and Central America and speak about 30 Mayan languages. Many still plant maize with prayers and keep the 260-day calendar. Their stories sit alongside those of peoples further north, from the turtle-backed world to Coyote's tricks, in [[@myths-native-american|Native American stories]].

text: A picture book is made by a small team. An author writes a short text, an illustrator plans and paints the pictures, an editor helps shape both, and a designer fits words and pictures onto each spread (two facing pages). Then the book is printed, folded, bound and shipped.

The hard part is the planning. Most picture books have just 32 pages, and the words are often under 1,000. So the makers think about every page turn like a film director thinks about every scene. What does the reader see first? What is hidden until the next page? That decision can make a child laugh out loud.

st.reveal: Books are printed on very large sheets, with many pages on each side. The sheet is folded and trimmed into a bundle of pages, and 32 is a cheap, tidy number to make. Some pages go to the title and copyright, which leaves about 28 for the story.

myth: Picture books are easy to write because they are short.
Every word has to earn its place, and the pictures must tell part of the story the words leave out. Authors often rewrite a picture book dozens of times before it is printed.

sec.h: Words that leave room for pictures

sec.t:
Illustrators start with tiny sketches called thumbnails, sometimes no bigger than a stamp, for all 32 pages at once. This shows how the whole book flows. Then they make a dummy: a rough mock-up of the book with pencil drawings, so the editor can turn the pages and feel the pace.

Only after many changes does the final art begin. Some artists paint with watercolour or cut paper. Eric Carle made *The Very Hungry Caterpillar* (1969) from tissue paper he had painted himself. Others now draw on a tablet. Indian publishers such as Tulika in Chennai often use folk styles like [[@gond-art|Gond]] and [[@warli|Warli]] painting.

Picture books are printed with four inks: cyan, magenta, yellow and black. Tiny dots of these four mix in your eye to make every other shade, which is why [[@colour-mix|colour mixing]] matters to printers. Big sheets carrying many pages at once rush through the press. They are folded, trimmed and stitched or glued into a hard cover.

The first copies are checked carefully, because a skin colour or a sky that comes out slightly wrong can spoil a page. Board books for babies get extra thought. Their pages are thick card with rounded corners, and the inks must be safe, because babies chew them.

From the first draft to the bookshop, a picture book often takes one to two years. A popular one may then be reprinted for decades, read by parents who first heard it as children themselves.

One of the earliest picture books for children was *Orbis Pictus* ("The World in Pictures"), made by the Czech teacher John Amos Comenius in 1658. It used woodcut pictures to teach Latin words. In 1902 Beatrix Potter's *The Tale of Peter Rabbit* showed how small, gentle paintings could carry a story.

Since 1938 the American Library Association has given the Caldecott Medal to the best American picture book each year. Maurice Sendak won it for *Where the Wild Things Are*. In India, Pratham Books puts thousands of free picture books online in many [[@languages-india|Indian languages]], so a child in a village can read a story in her own mother tongue.

text: The mid-day meal scheme gives a [[@lunch-world|free cooked lunch]] to children in government and government-aided schools across India. Since 2021 it has been called PM POSHAN. It feeds more than 10 crore children on school days, in more than 10 lakh schools.

A typical meal might be rice or roti with dal and vegetables. Some states add eggs, milk, fruit or millets. The idea is simple: children who are not [[@hunger|hungry]] can learn better, and families are more likely to send children to school when a meal is waiting there.

Every child in the covered classes at government and government-aided schools can eat the mid-day meal, whatever their family earns. Sharing the same food also helps children from different backgrounds eat together.

sec.t:
The idea started small. In 1925 the Madras city corporation began giving meals to poor children at some of its schools. In the 1950s and 1960s, K. Kamaraj, Chief Minister of Madras State, spread free school lunches widely, hoping more children would come to class.

In 1982 Chief Minister M. G. Ramachandran expanded it into a very large noon meal scheme in Tamil Nadu. Gujarat and Kerala ran their own programmes too. The national scheme started on 15 August 1995, though at first many states handed out dry grain instead of hot food.

Researchers have studied the scheme for decades. Many studies found that school meals helped raise attendance, especially among girls and children from poorer families. Some found children grew taller and healthier, and that eating together helped break down old barriers of caste.

The scheme also has problems. Some schools have poor kitchens, money arrives late, or meals lack enough [[@food-nutrients|nutrients]]. In 2013 contaminated food at a school in Bihar killed 23 children, which led to stricter safety checks. Whether to serve eggs has been debated in several states, because some families are vegetarian.

In many villages, local cooks prepare meals in each school. In cities, big central kitchens often take over. The Akshaya Patra Foundation, which began in [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]] in 2000, runs kitchens with huge steam cauldrons and conveyor belts. Each [[@maths-recipes-scale|kitchen cooks many thousands of meals]] every morning, and trucks deliver them to schools in time for lunch.

Menus vary from state to state, and that is deliberate, because local food is cheaper and children are more likely to eat what they know. Karnataka serves dishes like bisi bele bath, and some districts have added ragi. [[@odisha|Odisha]] and Tamil Nadu serve eggs on several days a week. Rajasthan has given children milk.

The government sets rules for how much grain, pulses, vegetables and oil each child should get. That way, the meal gives a fair share of the energy and protein a growing child needs in a day.

The United States has its own programme. In 1946 President Harry Truman signed the National School Lunch Act. Today the programme serves lunch to about 30 million children on a typical school day. Children from families with lower incomes eat for free or at a reduced price, and some schools serve free meals to everyone.

The menus are very different, with milk cartons and [[@food-sandwich-name|sandwiches]] instead of sambar and rice. But the idea is the same one Madras tried a century ago. A hungry child cannot learn much.
